subject: ent
title: Deep neck space infections

steps.tx: Deep neck infections spread from the **lower molar teeth**, tonsils, salivary glands or foreign bodies and travel along **fascial planes** toward the airway, mediastinum, carotid artery and jugular vein. **Ludwig angina** is a bilateral submandibular cellulitis, usually from infected lower molars, that produces a woody floor of mouth with a raised tongue, drooling and stridor. Secure the airway first, then obtain contrast CT when safe, give antibiotics, drain surgically and remove the dental source.
steps.say: Ludwig angina starts from an infected lower molar tooth and spreads into the floor of the mouth on both sides. The floor feels woody and hard, and it pushes the tongue upward toward the palate. The patient drools saliva because swallowing becomes painful and difficult. This swelling can close the airway quickly, so doctors secure breathing before ordering any scan. Treatment combines strong antibiotics with surgical drainage and removal of the infected tooth.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram showing deep neck fascial spaces, their connections, and potential pathways for infection spread.
vis.caption: Deep neck spaces and potential infection spread

steps.tx: **Retropharyngeal abscess** mainly strikes young children whose nasopharyngeal nodes are still present, causing fever, neck stiffness, torticollis, drooling and stridor that mimic epiglottitis or meningitis, while adult cases follow foreign body perforation, trauma or vertebral osteomyelitis. **Parapharyngeal abscess** shows trismus, medial tonsil displacement and neck swelling, and endangers the carotid sheath through **jugular thrombosis**, carotid blowout and lower cranial nerve palsies. Pharyngitis followed by a septic jugular clot in an adolescent means **Lemierre syndrome**.
steps.say: Retropharyngeal abscess occurs mainly in small children and causes fever with a stiff painful neck. The child holds the neck tilted to one side and drools saliva continuously. Noisy breathing or stridor appears when the pus pocket presses the airway backward. Parapharyngeal abscess blocks jaw opening and displaces the tonsil toward the midline. A teenager who develops a tender neck swelling with fever after a sore throat may carry an infected jugular clot.

steps.tx: The axial scan shows a large rim enhancing **retropharyngeal collection** that pushes the pharyngeal wall forward and squeezes the **carotid sheath**. This matches the abscess step where fever with neck stiffness and drooling in a small child signals danger. In the exam, link a widened prevertebral space with urgent **contrast CT** and theatre airway control, since rupture can flood the mediastinum and cause **descending mediastinitis**.
steps.say: This axial scan presents a large dark collection behind the pharynx that pushes the throat wall forward and squeezes the carotid sheath. The picture explains why a stiff neck with drooling in a small child remains an emergency. Such collections require urgent contrast imaging and a secured airway in theatre. Rupture allows pus to track downward and produce a deadly chest infection.

vis.alt: Axial neck CT showing a large rim enhancing retropharyngeal collection displacing the pharyngeal wall and compressing the carotid sheath.
vis.caption: Axial CT showing retropharyngeal collection displacing pharyngeal wall. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: When the airway is unstable the patient goes to theatre for securing with fibreoptic intubation or tracheostomy under local anaesthesia before imaging. Stable patients undergo **contrast CT** of the neck, extended to the chest when **descending mediastinitis** is suspected from chest pain, crepitus or a widened mediastinum, and this chest spread carries high mortality and needs thoracic drainage. **Necrotising fasciitis** shows pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus and rapid spread, especially in diabetic hosts, and demands immediate wide debridement, not antibiotics alone.
steps.say: An unstable airway always takes priority over imaging in every suspected deep neck infection. Doctors depend on the operating theatre to control the airway before the patient moves anywhere else. Stable patients need a contrast scan of the neck that shows the pus collection. Doctors extend the scan to the chest when pain or crackling under the skin suggests spread downward. Rapidly spreading infection with severe pain and blisters needs urgent wide surgical removal of dead tissue.

steps.tx: Vigilance must continue after drainage because **carotid blowout** often announces itself with a small sentinel bleed, while jugular thrombophlebitis throws **septic emboli** to the lungs and pus can track into the mediastinum or spill into the airway. Complete care adds **source control** through tooth extraction, foreign body removal or tonsil drainage pathways, culture directed antibiotics covering streptococci, anaerobes and staphylococci, and close HDU monitoring. Diabetes and immunocompromise lower the threshold for imaging and surgery.
steps.say: Doctors keep watching the patient closely even after draining the neck swelling. A small warning bleed from the wound can signal a major carotid rupture ahead. Infected clots in the jugular vein can break off and travel toward the lungs. Removing the original cause remains essential, so doctors extract the bad tooth or remove the foreign body. Cultures guide the antibiotic choice, and nurses monitor the patient in a high dependency unit.
